note.note:
Subjective:
- Presenting complaint and trigger/exposure: Sudden‐onset dizziness/“room spinning” with associated nausea while preparing breakfast at home this morning.
- Symptom timeline and progression: Began ≈2 h ago; continuous since onset. Similar but brief episode 1 mo ago (5–10 min, self-resolved).
- ENT symptoms: 
  • Ear buzzing/tinnitus bilaterally (no ear pain, discharge, or hearing loss).  
  • No throat tightness, voice change, dysphagia, drooling, nasal/ocular symptoms, stridor, dyspnea, facial/oral swelling, ear pain, or neck pain.
- Relevant past episodes and treatments: Prior short vertigo episode 1 mo ago; no previous evaluations, hospital visits, or injections.
- Allergies and current medications: 
  • Allergies: Denies drug/food allergies.  
  • Medications: Hormone-replacement therapy for premature ovarian failure (dose/route/frequency not documented). New prescription for vertigo medication (name not captured in transcript) 1 tablet TID ×10 days.
- Any relevant social context: At home; husband present (patient was making him breakfast).

Objective:
- Observable swelling/distribution: Not reported.
- Airway/breathing: No stridor or respiratory distress reported.
- Mental status/associated features: Alert; reports dizziness and unsteadiness, no focal weakness or speech changes.
- Vitals and examination findings: Not recorded (video consult; formal neuro/ENT exam pending).
- Presence of another person: Husband in household (not on call).

Assessment:
- Working impression: Acute vestibular syndrome most consistent with labyrinthitis/vestibular neuritis.
  • Evidence: Sudden continuous vertigo lasting hours, tinnitus, gait unsteadiness, absence of focal neurologic deficits or hearing loss, no recent viral prodrome but fits typical presentation.
- Differential diagnoses (aligned with DDx):
  1. Vestibular neuritis / viral labyrinthitis – High likelihood; matches acute persistent vertigo + tinnitus, no focal deficits. Opposing: no preceding URI, no hearing loss (supports neuritis variant).
  2. Ménière’s disease – Moderate; recurrent vertigo and tinnitus, but lacks fluctuating hearing loss and typical episode length.  
  3. Posterior-circulation stroke/TIA – Low-medium; acute vertigo and imbalance could signify cerebellar ischemia; no focal signs and age 42 with no risk factors reduce likelihood.
- No conflicts noted between transcript and DDx.

Plan:
- Pharmacologic: Sent electronic prescription to Lloyds Pharmacy for vertigo symptom control (medication name inaudible in transcript) 1 tablet three times daily for 10 days.
- Follow-up care: Patient to schedule in-person appointment with primary-care/ENT provider within next few days for otoscopic exam, vital signs, gait/neuro assessment, and consideration of further work-up (e.g., vestibular testing, audiogram).
- Safety / escalation instructions:
  • Call emergency services (999/A&E) immediately for any new limb weakness, facial droop, severe headache, slurred speech, difficulty walking, inability to keep down fluids, persistent vomiting, or worsening vertigo.
  • If symptoms significantly worsen before scheduled review, attend A&E.
- Self-care: May take prescribed medication with or without food; OK to take on waking if nauseated. Avoid driving or operating machinery until symptoms resolve. Remain accompanied at home while unsteady.

Quality checks (document_quality):
● Missing expected elements: vital signs, full neurological examination, formal audiologic assessment, exact name/dose of prescribed medication, precise HRT regimen, complete allergy list (environmental/food), social history (smoking/alcohol), safety screening (falls risk), documentation of head-movement provocation tests (e.g., Dix-Hallpike).  
● Conflicts between transcript and DDx: None identified.  
● Transcript quality: Generally clear; medication name was inaudible/untranscribed, and minor background noise.
